input:
This memo recommends that a three-month pilot of condition sensors should be carried out before any decision is taken on installing sensors across the whole plant. The plant operates a total of 214 pumps. Maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show 1321 h of unplanned downtime, and it is notable that bearing failures account for 45% of the downtime hours.

A sensor set for all 214 pumps has been quoted at $414k installed, plus a further $76k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 24%; however, it should be emphasised that this is a vendor figure and that it was not measured at this plant, where conditions may be different in various respects. A pilot on 16 pumps would cost $34k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so the pilot would test the detection benefit only, rather than any improvement in repair times.

The memo therefore recommends the three-month pilot, covering 16 pumps in the first instance. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results have been reported and can be considered by the review in due course.

In addition, it should be borne in mind that the downtime record itself provides the baseline against which any improvement would be judged, and the pilot would allow that comparison to be made on a consistent basis, under the plant's own operating and maintenance conditions, rather than relying on results obtained elsewhere under conditions that may differ in material respects.
target:
A three-month pilot of condition sensors on 16 pumps is recommended. The decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported, and the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review.

The plant runs 214 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1321 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 45% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $414k installed, plus $76k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 24%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, and it carries the trial's conditions with it: a comparable unit is not this plant, and the trial's maintenance regime is not stated in the figure.

The pilot is sized to the failure mode that dominates the record. Bearing failure is the largest single share of downtime hours, and it is the mode the sensors detect, so a pilot that runs long enough to catch bearing failures in progress tests the claim on which the full expenditure rests. A pilot on 16 pumps at $34k over three months buys the plant's own downtime evidence at a small fraction of the full installed cost. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so any reduction the pilot shows comes from earlier warning, not from faster repair, and the two effects are not confounded in the pilot's figures. The capital review decides on full installation with the pilot's reported downtime in hand, and a pilot that shows no reduction ends the proposal at pilot cost.
